Medial Nagel

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move a triangle's corners and watch three lines keep meeting at one spot.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Press Show hint for matching tick marks, and Check the claim to test your triangle.
Look for the math

The original page states: “Let EDF be the medial triangle of ABC. The incircles of triangles AEF, BDF, and CDE are tangent to EF, FD, and DE at P, Q, R, respectively. Prove that DP, EQ, FR are concurrent. Furthermore, the point of concurrency is the Nagel point of DEF.” Drag the corners: the three red lines always cross at the same yellow dot M.

Three copies of one triangle

Join the middles of the sides of ABC to make its medial triangle DEF. The corner triangles AEF, BDF and CDE are half-size translates of ABC and of each other. Each has an incircle that touches the inner side at P, Q or R. The logic test recomputes those touch points from side lengths and finds the same P, Q, R in every one of more than six thousand triangles.

Equal lengths make the lines meet

Two tangents drawn from one point to the same circle have equal lengths, so the overlapping corner triangles give ER = FQ, DR = FP and DQ = EP. Multiplying the three ratios (EP/PF) · (FQ/QD) · (DR/RE) = 1 and applying Ceva's theorem proves that DP, EQ and FR pass through one point. Press Show hint to see the equal pairs marked with one, two and three strokes.

A point that splits perimeters

Write s = (EF + FD + DE) / 2. The touch points satisfy EF + ER = DF + DR = s, and the same is true around the other two sides. A point on a side with this property is where an excircle of DEF touches that side, so P, Q and R are exactly the excircle touch points, and their cevians meet at the Nagel point of DEF. Show excircles draws those three circles; the logic test checks all three perimeter equations and the excircle contacts over the whole sample, with no counterexample.

The two other centres

The incircle of DEF touches the same sides at P′, Q′ and R′. Each is the mirror image of P, Q or R in the midpoint of its side: for instance P and P′ are equally far from the ends of EF. So the cevians through them meet at the Gergonne point G, the isotomic conjugate of the Nagel point M. Finally, ABC is the anticomplementary triangle of DEF, so M is also the incenter of ABC. The original page shows three copies of the applet with different checkboxes; this one keeps all four switches and starts with names and the incircle showing. There is no win or loss: Press Check the claim to finish exploring.

Press Show hint, then pull A close to B. The one-, two- and three-stroke marks still match, until the triangle is too thin to draw its incircles.
